items.title: Caste is a complex social hierarchy with religious framings
items.claim: How does the caste system relate to Hindu religion?

options.text: It is purely social with no religious dimension

Varna (the fourfold theoretical division — Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, Shudras) is described in the Vedas and the Manusmriti; jati (thousands of birth-based occupational groupings) is the lived reality; modern reform movements (Ambedkar, Gandhi, contemporary Dalit activism) have contested its religious basis
Caste was invented by British colonisers

items.reveal:
The Rig Veda's Purusha Sukta (10.90) describes the four varnas emerging from a cosmic being. The Manusmriti (c. 200 BCE-200 CE) codifies caste duties.

Dalits (formerly 'untouchables') were treated as outside the varna system. B.R. Ambedkar (1891-1956), Dalit leader and chief architect of India's constitution, converted to Buddhism in 1956 partly to escape caste. The Indian Constitution (1950) outlaws untouchability.

The relationship between varna theory and the thousands of jatis on the ground is complex. Caste discrimination persists in many forms — the UK Equality Act 2010 includes caste under race discrimination provisions.
items.why: Religious texts and social systems interact in ways that resist clean separation. The caste case shows how a religious tradition can be deployed for social hierarchy and also generate its own critics.

items.title: The Five Pillars have a canonical order — beginning with Shahada
items.claim: What is the standard Sunni order of the Five Pillars of Islam?

options.text: Shahada (declaration of faith), Salah (five daily prayers), Zakat (almsgiving, 2.5% of accumulated wealth), Sawm (fasting in Ramadan), Hajj (pilgrimage to Mecca, once if able)

items.reveal:
The Hadith of Gabriel (recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim) lists the Pillars in this order. The Shahada is the doorway — 'There is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God'.

Shia Islam (Twelver tradition) frames obligations differently. They recognise the practices but as part of the Furu al-Din (Ten Ancillaries of the Religion), alongside jihad, enjoining good and forbidding wrong, tawalla (love of the household of the Prophet) and tabarra (disassociation from enemies).

Zakat is calculated annually on accumulated wealth above a threshold (nisab); Sawm requires no food, drink or marital relations from dawn (fajr) to sunset (maghrib) during Ramadan.
items.why: Religious practice has specific structure. Treating the Pillars as a vague list of good acts misses the theological logic — faith first, then prayer, then social action.

items.title: Ten human Sikh Gurus, then the eternal Guru Granth Sahib
items.claim: How does the Sikh tradition handle leadership after Guru Gobind Singh?

options.text: It ended with the tenth Guru with no continuation
In 1708 Guru Gobind Singh declared the Guru Granth Sahib (the scripture) to be the eternal Guru — no further human gurus
It continues through a hereditary line

items.reveal:
Guru Gobind Singh died in 1708 from a stab wound inflicted by an Afghan assassin. Before his death he installed the Adi Granth (compiled by Guru Arjan in 1604) as Guru Granth Sahib — making the scripture the eternal Guru.

The Guru Granth Sahib (1,430 pages, mostly in Gurmukhi script) contains hymns by six of the ten Gurus, plus 15 Hindu and Muslim saints (bhagats) — including Kabir and Sheikh Farid. It is treated as a living Guru: bowed to, awakened in the morning, put to rest at night.

Sikh gurdwaras place the Guru Granth Sahib on a throne (palki) as the central focus.
items.why: The structural innovation of designating scripture as eternal Guru ended succession disputes that plague many religions. Sikh community continuity rests on the text, not on a living hierarchy.
